explanations.explanation: True, friend. Jesus says, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted." (Matthew 5:4) Comfort is the promise, right there in the line. I think this one is tender, so I'll leave it simple and let it sit.

Take another look, friend. Jesus says, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted." (Matthew 5:4) The promise is comfort, and it's stated right in the line. I think that's a tender thing to hear when your heart is heavy.

explanations.answer: Who is blessed and what they'll get
explanations.explanation: That's the pattern. The poor in spirit get "the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 5:3), and those who mourn "will be comforted" (Matthew 5:4). Same cutter, different dough. Spot the shape once and you can spot it down the whole list.

explanations.answer: What to do and what to avoid
explanations.explanation: Neither line hands out a to-do or a not-to-do. Jesus names a group, calls them blessed, then tells what's coming to them (Matthew 5:3, 5:4). Nothing in those two lines is a command, friend. It's all promise.

explanations.answer: A question and then its answer
explanations.explanation: No questions in those two lines, friend. Each one is a plain statement: a group is blessed and a promise follows (Matthew 5:3, 5:4). Jesus does ask a question later in this sermon, about salt (Matthew 5:13), but that's down the road.
Filled. Jesus says, "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled." (Matthew 5:6) Not a nibble, not a crumb, filled. No half-empty cookie jar in that promise.
Tested is a fair guess, since hard things do come up in this sermon. But it's not the word in this line. Jesus says those who hunger and thirst for righteousness "will be filled." (Matthew 5:6)
Humbled doesn't show up in this line, friend. Jesus says they "will be filled." (Matthew 5:6) Hungry and thirsty first, then filled. I like how that ends.
Jesus says the opposite. "Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy." (Matthew 5:7) There's a promise attached, and it's mercy. Every line in this stretch comes with one.
Right, it's false. Jesus says, "Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy." (Matthew 5:7) They're called blessed and given a promise in the same breath. Blessed AND promised, friend.
Pure. "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God." (Matthew 5:8) Jesus goes straight to the heart, not the apron or the hat. And the promise is a big one: they will see God.

Proud is a sneaky one, friend, and I've puffed up over a nice straight row of cookies myself. But the word here is pure: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God." (Matthew 5:8) That one word changes the whole line.

Bold sounds like a cookie with extra chocolate chips, and I respect that. But Jesus says pure: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God." (Matthew 5:8) The line is about the heart, and the promise is seeing God.
The peacemakers. Jesus says, "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God." (Matthew 5:9) That's a name worth having, friend. He gives it to the ones who make peace.
Scribes aren't in this passage at all. Jesus says, "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God." (Matthew 5:9) That name goes to the peacemakers.

Shepherds don't come up anywhere in this passage, friend. It's a fine job, but the line says, "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God." (Matthew 5:9) That one goes to the peacemakers.

Righteousness. Jesus says, "Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." (Matthew 5:10) I think this is one of the heavier lines in the sermon, so I'll say it plain. Jesus names the reason, and He names the promise too.

Lawlessness isn't the word in this line, friend. Jesus says persecuted "because of righteousness." (Matthew 5:10) I think this is a heavy one, so I'll keep it simple: the reason is righteousness, and the promise is the kingdom of heaven.

Foolishness isn't the word in this line, friend. Jesus says they're persecuted "because of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." (Matthew 5:10) I think it's a heavy line. The reason is righteousness, and a promise comes with it.

True. In Matthew 5:3, the poor in spirit hear, "for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." In Matthew 5:10, those persecuted because of righteousness hear those very same words. Same promise on the first line and the eighth. I think it's a sturdy one to hold.

Take another look, friend. Matthew 5:3 says, "for theirs is the kingdom of heaven," and Matthew 5:10 says it again for those persecuted because of righteousness. Same promise at both ends of the list. I think it's a heavy line, and the promise in it is a steady one.

Rejoice and be glad. Jesus says, "Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven…" (Matthew 5:12) I think that's a heavy thing to be told, and Jesus gives the reason in the same line. Great is the reward in heaven.

Weeping and being still isn't what Jesus says here, friend. After the insults and the persecution, He says, "Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven…" (Matthew 5:12) I think this is a heavy line. The reason comes right with it.

Fleeing and hiding aren't in these verses, friend. Jesus says, "Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven…" (Matthew 5:12) I think it's heavy to be insulted and persecuted, which makes that line land harder.
Heaven. Jesus says, "Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven…" (Matthew 5:12) The reward is great, and Jesus says where it is. That's the reason He gives for rejoicing.

The land isn't in this line, friend. Jesus does say the meek will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5), but here He says "great is your reward in heaven." (Matthew 5:12) Different promise, different address.
The temple isn't mentioned anywhere in these verses, friend. Jesus says, "great is your reward in heaven." (Matthew 5:12) Heaven it is.
True. Jesus says, "for in the same way they persecuted the prophets before you." (Matthew 5:12) I think that's a heavy line. It also tells His listeners that others walked this road before them.

Jesus says the opposite. "For in the same way they persecuted the prophets before you." (Matthew 5:12) The prophets came before His listeners, and they were persecuted in the same way. I think it might be a comfort that others walked this road first, but that's my guess.

Thrown out and trampled. Jesus says salt that loses its savor is "no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled by men." (Matthew 5:13) Salt without its saltiness has exactly one job left, and it's getting stepped on. Rough ending for salt, friend.

Mixing in fresh salt is a clever idea, but Jesus never mentions it. He asks how salt that lost its savor can be made salty again. Then He says it's "no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled by men." (Matthew 5:13)

explanations.answer: It's dried out in the sun
explanations.explanation: Drying out in the sun doesn't come up in this verse, friend. I've left cookies on a windowsill and watched them dry out, but that's cookies. For the salt, Jesus says it's "no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled by men." (Matthew 5:13)

Jesus says the opposite. "A city on a hill cannot be hidden." (Matthew 5:14) Trying to hide one would be like hiding a fresh batch from a hungry house, because the smell gives it away. No amount of effort changes what Jesus says.
False, friend. "A city on a hill cannot be hidden." (Matthew 5:14) Jesus says cannot, with no fine print. Trying harder doesn't change it.
On a stand. Jesus says, "Instead, they set it on a stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house." (Matthew 5:15) One lamp, one stand, a whole house lit up. No basket in sight.

A bed isn't in this verse, friend. Jesus says people set the lamp "on a stand" instead. (Matthew 5:15) A lamp under a bed would mostly light up dust bunnies and one lost sock. On the stand, it gives light to everyone in the house.

An inner room isn't in this verse, friend. Jesus says, "Instead, they set it on a stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house." (Matthew 5:15) Everyone in the house, not just whoever is standing in one room.

Deeds. Jesus says, "let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds…" (Matthew 5:16) Good deeds, friend, the kind of thing people can actually see. That's what the light is shining on.
Clothes aren't the word, friend. Jesus says people will see your good "deeds." (Matthew 5:16) My apron is spotless, but it's not the light in this verse.
Fortune isn't in this verse. Jesus says people will see your good "deeds." (Matthew 5:16) He points to what people do, not what they have. Good news for someone who owns more crumbs than coins.

Their Father in heaven. Jesus says, "let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven." (Matthew 5:16) The light shines, people see the good deeds, and the glory goes to the Father. The verse ends pointing up, friend.

The prophets come up earlier in this passage, as people who were persecuted (Matthew 5:12). But they're not who people glorify in verse 16. Jesus says people "glorify your Father in heaven." (Matthew 5:16)
Kings of the earth aren't in these verses, friend. Jesus says people "glorify your Father in heaven." (Matthew 5:16) Nobody in that verse needs a crown. It wouldn't fit over my chef's hat anyway.
